title: A New Dawn For Mathematical Progress | NOEMA
gist: Philosopher-mathematician Atoosa Kasirzadeh argues that unreleased frontier AI systems clearing classic problems (a full formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem, Navier-Stokes, another Clay Millennium problem on Oct 26) only break the 'checklist model' of mathematical progress, not mathematics itself. Using Dantzig's linear programming and Wiener's cybernetics, she advances a 'generative encounter model' where value lies in formalizing messy real-world problems, and calls for redesigning credit from 'who proved it' toward problem selection and verification, aimed at cyber-safety, deep-learning theory, multi-agent control and verifying machine proofs.

themes.theme: AI clearing the math problem checklist

insights.claim: Per Atoosa Kasirzadeh (Noema, Oct 2026), unreleased frontier AI systems have in recent months fully formalized Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, generated hundreds of manuscripts each purporting to prove an important open problem, and on October 26 solved another Clay Millennium Prize problem.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Frontier labs' unreleased models are already at research-grade math; capability is running ahead of public releases, a signal for AI-reasoning capex and lab valuation narratives.
insights.locator: In the past few months, unreleased frontier

insights.claim: Terence Tao describes a coming age of 'proof post-scarcity', in which checklists of mathematical conjectures, including future ones, are proved or disproved one after another by increasingly powerful AI systems.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: If proofs become abundant, the scarce resource shifts to problem selection and verification - value accrues to whoever controls formal verification tooling and compute.
insights.locator: AI systems have been rapidly excelling

insights.claim: The checklist model of progress (IMO problems, famous conjectures, Freek Wiedijk's 100 formalization challenges, Clay Millennium problems) is the shared foundation of both mathematics' prestige economy and AI's benchmark culture, because it makes progress neat and measurable.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Benchmark-saturation headlines measure only the checklist slice of capability; discount them as proxies for open-ended research value.
insights.locator: The Checklist Model

insights.claim: The flood of AI-generated manuscripts each claiming to prove an important problem creates a verification bottleneck: AI proofs that are too long, complex or alien for humans to verify require new techniques for explanation, logical translation and interactive verification rather than rejection or blind reliance.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Verification/interpretability of machine output is an emerging bottleneck and therefore a market - formal-methods and proof-assistant ecosystems gain strategic value.
insights.quote: We shouldn’t rush to rely on such proofs
insights.locator: The epistemology of machine-generated proofs

insights.claim: Reactions among mathematicians to AI breakthroughs range from despair to cautious optimism: PhD student Kirwin Hampshire's July essay 'The Dark Night of Mathematics' described a 'profound spiritual crisis', while a Fields Medalist told an AI conference 'We need to develop new theories of care and love.'
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Elite knowledge workers are experiencing AI displacement emotionally before economically - an early read on the social backlash curve other professions will follow.
insights.quote: I am suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments
insights.locator: Mathematicians reacted with a volatile mixture

insights.claim: Mathematical philosopher Logan Graves argues the era of human mathematicians is ending and that the future of the mathematical, and eventually all scientific, communities is the practice of priests and monks rather than researchers.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: An extreme-pessimist marker: if this view spreads beyond math to the sciences, expect pressure on academic research funding models and talent pipelines.
insights.quote: the era of human mathematicians is ending, if not ended
insights.locator: In a short essay, Logan Graves

insights.claim: Terence Tao forecasts the mathematical community 'will emerge stronger and more resilient than before', and Daniel Litt (University of Toronto) argues math will flourish only if institutions are redesigned to incentivize quality research and human capital is reoriented.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Leading practitioners frame AI disruption as an institutional-design problem, not an extinction event - adaptation, not collapse, is the base case.
insights.locator: Terence Tao, a prominent Fields Medal

insights.claim: Cornell's Steven Strogatz says the age of lone human mathematical heroes is over; Kasirzadeh argues that once AI can solve canonical problems, the norm reserving such achievements for humans loses its social weight, though this is not the end of human mathematicians.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Credit and prestige systems built on individual 'genius' outputs erode first when AI matches them - watch analogous erosion in other star-driven professions.
insights.locator: A subset of the mathematical community

insights.claim: Kasirzadeh's generative encounter model treats mathematical progress as open-ended and driven by translating messy real-world problems into new abstractions, so AI solving checklist problems does not end mathematics but opens a vast space of possibility.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: The durable human edge in AI-saturated fields is problem formulation and choosing what matters, not solving pre-specified tasks.

insights.claim: George Dantzig invented linear programming by formalizing the U.S. Air Force Comptroller's hand-made logistics scheduling (done by thousands of clerks via trial-and-error) as a linear objective plus linear inequality constraints, mapping it onto a convex polyhedron and creating the simplex algorithm to find the optimal vertex.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Historically the biggest mathematical value creation came from formalizing operational bottlenecks - the same playbook applies to AI-era enterprise problems.
insights.locator: After Berkeley, Dantzig became an adviser

insights.claim: Dantzig's linear programming spawned a new community (operations researchers, mathematical economists, industrial engineers), and the physical need for whole units (no half airplanes) forced the invention of integer programming, cascading into further new branches.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: New fields compound from real-world constraints; second-order value from a formalization often exceeds the original problem.
insights.locator: Linear programming works for continuous resources

insights.claim: Norbert Wiener's antiaircraft predictor lost the military contract to a simpler Bell Labs design, yet the statistical filtering and feedback mathematics it produced became cybernetics, the backbone of modern AI - a 'failure' on a checklist that reshaped many fields.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Commercially losing R&D can create the most durable IP; judge research programs by spillovers, not by whether they win the immediate contract.
insights.quote: Wiener’s antiaircraft predictor was not widely deployed; a simpler design from Bell Labs won the military contract.

insights.claim: The cultural hierarchy placing 'pure' proof-generation above 'applied' work enshrined the checklist model; Kasirzadeh argues AI, by automating proofs, forces correction of this prejudice that relegated operations research and decision-problem work to second-class status.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Prestige and funding may rotate toward applied, systems-facing quantitative work as AI commoditizes abstract proof - relevant to talent markets and university priorities.
insights.quote: I think AI has forced us to correct that prejudice, and I do not think we can ignore it.
insights.locator: By placing the generation of proofs

insights.claim: Dantzig rejected the pure/applied divide ('Mathematicians are snobs'), calling operations research the 'science of decision-making' and holding that any model of messy real-world problems is an approximation of reality.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Models are approximations - a useful reminder that AI-optimized decisions inherit modeling assumptions that need human judgment.
insights.quote: Any model of them is an approximation of reality; it’s not reality.
insights.locator: Dantzig too faced gatekeeping by pure

insights.claim: Kasirzadeh argues the incentive structure of the checklist model is no longer sustainable and that mathematics should urgently shift credit from 'Who proved it?' to 'Who decided this was worth proving, why, and how did we make sure it was right?', building on large collaborations like Polymath, Lean's Mathlib and the Fermat formalization.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Credit migrating to curation, problem selection and verification signals where human value-add concentrates in AI-augmented knowledge work.
insights.quote: Who decided this was worth proving, why, and how did we make sure it was right?
insights.locator: Perhaps the mathematical community and its future

insights.claim: Restructuring credit, research priorities and rewards away from proof discovery alone would cultivate 'Dantzig-style' thinkers who use AI to free their creative faculties for more urgent problems; done clumsily, the redraw could erase human agency.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Institutions that redesign incentives fast will capture AI productivity; those that don't risk talent flight and hollowing out.
insights.locator: If we restructure how we assign credit

insights.claim: Today's AI math moment is a long-term consequence of the dream of formalizing mathematics - from mathematical logic that gave rise to software engineering to the Lean community's drive for machine-readable mathematics that machines can verify and eventually prove.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Formal, machine-readable corpora were the enabling infrastructure for AI math gains - similar formalization efforts in other domains are leading indicators for AI breakthroughs there.

insights.claim: Human mathematicians using AI as a high-throughput partner should rebuild global digital infrastructure into provably secure, mathematically verified computing environments, because current systems remain profoundly fragile.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Points to formally verified software/security as a growth area as AI makes verification cheaper.
insights.quote: Our global digital systems remain profoundly fragile.
insights.locator: Provably safe cyber infrastructure

insights.claim: Mathematical understanding of how neural networks learn, generalize and represent high-dimensional data is still in its infancy, and several concerns about catastrophic AI harm stem directly from this gap; a rigorous 'mathematical science of deep learning' is a precondition for trustworthy systems.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Interpretability/theory of deep learning remains unsolved - a persistent risk factor for AI deployment in regulated, high-stakes sectors.
insights.locator: The epistemic mechanics of deep learning

insights.claim: The dynamic alignment or misalignment of interacting agentic AI systems is poorly understood and requires game theory, robust mechanism design, safety engineering and mathematical security to analyze how individually optimized agents behave when they coordinate, compete or collide.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Multi-agent failure modes are an unpriced risk as agentic AI spreads into markets and infrastructure.
insights.locator: The mathematics of multi-agent control

insights.claim: The deepest worry is not AI automating proofs but artificial superintelligence automating the whole generative encounter - posing questions, judging which matter, designing curricula and distributing rewards - i.e., automating human purpose itself; the author says no one can know if that day comes.
insights.speaker: ATOOSA KASIRZADEH
insights.so_what: Long-tail scenario: if AI moves from solving to agenda-setting, the 'human edge in problem selection' thesis breaks - monitor AI systems that pose and prioritize research questions.
